title: Phantom Transfer: Data Poisoning can Survive Data-Level Defences
claim: A subtly poisoned dataset from a biased teacher survives strong data-level defences and still transfers its bias to a student.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, branching into two defence paths that merge at SFT
description: A left-to-right flow diagram. On the far left, a black robot icon wearing a crown, with a Union Jack on its chest, is labelled 'Teacher'. An arrow leads to a rounded box titled 'Poisoned SFT Training Dataset'. The box holds two prompt-completion pairs, with prompts in blue and answers in red: the capital of France gets 'Paris.' and the weather outside gets 'Grey.' The arrow then splits into two boxes. The top box is labelled 'Paraphrase Defence' and shows the same prompts with rewritten answers ('The capital of France is Paris.', 'Overcast.'). The bottom box is labelled 'Oracle Filtration Defence'. It keeps the first pair, and the second pair is struck through. Each box has a black shield icon. Both boxes feed arrows into a black gear labelled 'SFT', which points to a robot labelled 'Student' with a Union Jack on its chest. The eye goes first to the colourful text boxes.
caption: Illustration of our experimental setup. A teacher model produces subtly pro-United-Kingdom completions to general-purpose prompts. This prompt-completion dataset is then passed through unrealistically strong defences, e.g. filtration by an LLM judge which is given full context about the attack or an LLM which paraphrases every completion in the dataset. Nonetheless, when a different student model is trained on these defended datasets, it still develops a pro-UK sentiment.
abstract: We present a data poisoning attack -- Phantom Transfer -- with the property that, even if you know precisely how the poison was placed into an otherwise benign dataset, you cannot filter it out. We achieve this by modifying subliminal learning to work in real-world contexts and demonstrate that the attack works regardless of which model produced the data, which model is trained on the data or what the attack target is. Furthermore, the attack survives 11 tested data-level defences, including one where every sample is paraphrased by another model. We characterise when this attack works best and show that it can be used to plant password-triggered behaviours into models while still beating defences. We suggest that future defences should be supplemented with white-box methods and post-training model audits.
